title: Blood glucose: build the control model
subtitle: Predict the response, test the mechanism and expose the model’s limits
objective: Explain the insulin response to raised blood glucose using a qualitative, controllable model.

sow.alignment: Directly develops C31 and Pearson7.13. Glucagon under7.14 is clearly labelled optional Higher-tier stretch and kept separate from the core interaction. No diagnosis, blood-glucose thresholds, treatment choices or dose calculations are included.

priorLearning: Hormones travel in blood to responsive tissues.
Glucose can be used in respiration.
Negative feedback reduces a departure from a regulated condition.
success: Sequence raised glucose → insulin release → target response → movement towards a suitable range.
Explain why a qualitative model cannot predict a person’s readings or treatment.

vocabulary.meaning: The amount of glucose in a stated volume of blood.
A hormone released by pancreatic beta cells that helps lower raised blood glucose through target-tissue responses.
A stored carbohydrate made from joined glucose units, especially in liver and muscle.
An organ with endocrine cells that release hormones including insulin.
A response that reduces the original departure from suitable conditions.
A model showing the kind or direction of a change rather than calibrated numerical predictions.

equipment: Shared evidence sheet, one selected response route, pen and ruler.
Projector or offline HTML/PowerPoint; calculator where useful.
preparation: Print the shared page, one selected response route and the exit page. Routes are alternatives, not extra tasks.
Read the worked answers and note any constructed data before teaching.
Use the core interaction first. Keep the Higher glucagon panel closed unless that extension is appropriate.
All displayed levels are qualitative labels. Do not substitute pupil readings, medicine amounts or clinical thresholds into this classroom model.
safety: Paper and screen lesson; no human sampling, exercise test, breath holding, medicine handling or personal health disclosure.
practicalAlternative: All evidence is supplied. Use paper diagrams and cards, pointing, annotation or dictation if a device is unavailable.

misconceptions.claim: Insulin is the same substance as glucose.
misconceptions.correction: Insulin is a hormone; glucose is a small sugar molecule.
misconceptions.check: Ask which is the message and which is a material used by cells.

misconceptions.correction: Insulin signals target processes; glucose units can be stored as glycogen.
misconceptions.check: Trace the hormone arrow separately from the glucose-material arrow.

misconceptions.claim: Every cell needs insulin for every glucose uptake process.
misconceptions.correction: Insulin affects particular target tissues; several tissues also take up glucose through insulin-independent routes.
misconceptions.check: Use “some body cells, such as muscle cells” in the core explanation.

misconceptions.claim: The model can tell someone their required insulin dose.
misconceptions.correction: It has no clinical measurements, individual parameters or treatment rules.
misconceptions.check: Ask which real-world information is deliberately absent.

access.supported: Same core concepts with chunked prompts and read-aloud access. Record support used; a pathway is not a diagnosis or fixed attainment label.
access.standard: Explain the supplied evidence independently using accurate scientific terms and units.
access.stretch: Optional deeper transfer or evaluation. Higher-tier-only material is labelled explicitly and is not required for the core outcome.
access.regulation: Offer solo or partner work, a quiet response, a pass and brief reset with clear re-entry. No forced disclosure or public performance.

slides.title: Build a model that explains a direction
body: What could reduce a rise in blood glucose?
We will model a mechanism, without medical numbers.
slides.notes: Invite prediction; reassure that no personal diet, health or medication disclosure is required.

slides.title: Message, material or store?
body: R1. What carries hormones around the body?
R2. What can cells use glucose for?
R3. What does negative feedback oppose?
slides.notes: R1: blood. R2: respiration and building/storing materials. R3: the original departure. Introduce glycogen as a store if the word is unfamiliar.

slides.title: Trace the core response
body: Raised glucose stimulates pancreatic beta cells.
More insulin is released into blood.
Responsive tissues change glucose handling.
slides.notes: Think aloud through the four-box model. Some body cells, such as muscle cells, increase uptake; liver and muscle storage as glycogen is promoted. Avoid saying every cell’s uptake always requires insulin.

visual.title: Raised glucose triggers a corrective response
visual.description: Core qualitative sequence: blood glucose rises after absorption; pancreatic beta cells release more insulin; responsive tissues increase uptake/storage processes; glucose concentration tends towards the usual suitable range. This is not a fixed-time or dose model.

slides.title: Follow the material separately from the signal
body: Insulin is a hormone signal.
Glucose units can be stored as glycogen.
The hormone does not become the store.
slides.notes: Trace purple signal arrow and orange material arrow separately. This is a molecule-role model, not a detailed chemical reaction mechanism.

visual.title: A signal is not the stored material
visual.description: Material-versus-signal model: insulin from pancreas signals liver/muscle storage processes. Separate glucose symbols are joined into a schematic glycogen store. Insulin does not become glycogen; molecule drawings are simplified.

elements.text: A signal is not the stored material
Insulin is a signal; glucose supplies the stored units.

slides.title: A direction model has a clear limit
body: The trace shows a rise and a corrective response.
It has no real time scale, concentration scale or dose rule.
slides.notes: Model: “Later is nearer the usual range in this conceptual trace. I cannot read a medical value, a time-to-recovery or treatment from it.” As glucose returns towards usual levels, the stimulus for extra insulin release reduces.

slides.title: Control-panel challenge
body: W1. Predict the next stage before advancing the model.
Explain the link from glucose rise to insulin release.
slides.notes: Use manual stage controls. Start with usual, then absorption/raised, insulin response, target response and towards usual. Paper alternative orders cards A–D.

body: W2. “Insulin is stored as glycogen.”
Replace the wrong substance and explain the hormone’s role.
slides.notes: Glucose units are stored as glycogen; insulin signals target processes. Ask which arrow carries the message and which carries material.

slides.title: Test what the model cannot claim
body: W3. Can the trace predict an exact reading after a meal?
Name the missing information.
slides.notes: No: no calibrated concentrations, times, personal physiology or meal quantities. It is designed for mechanism and direction only.

slides.title: Which response belongs in the core model?
body: Choose a causal sequence.
slides.notes: First option correct. If pupil swaps insulin/glucose, return to the two-arrow diagram.

options.text: Raised glucose → more insulin release → uptake/storage responses.
options.feedback: This is the core corrective pathway for raised blood glucose.

options.text: Insulin becomes glucose, so blood glucose rises further.
options.feedback: Insulin is a signal, not a sugar product.

options.text: The picture supplies an exact medicine dose.
options.feedback: There are no clinical measurements or dose rules in this model.

slides.title: Create the explanation that sits behind the controls
body: Choose your agreed route.
Core: insulin response. Higher extension: separate glucagon branch.
slides.notes: Keep the Higher branch optional and visually distinct. Do not require it for core success.

slides.title: Predict, explain and state a limit
body: Use the qualitative sequence and role diagram.
Make one correction to a misleading claim.
slides.notes: Supported S1–S4; standard M1–M4; stretch T1–T4. T3 is optional Higher glucagon; other evaluation is not a tier label.

slides.title: Audience: which arrow is the message?
body: L1. Share one explanation.
Audience asks which substance is signalling and which is stored.
slides.notes: Pupil traces or labels the two arrows; quiet partner/TA review is acceptable.

slides.title: An accurate model is deliberately bounded
body: It explains a feedback mechanism.
It does not diagnose a condition or prescribe an action.
slides.notes: Restate that qualitative usual/raised labels are not clinical categories for any pupil.

slides.title: Keep the roles distinct
body: E1. Which organ releases insulin?
E2. What is stored as glycogen?
E3. Why can this model not predict a dose?
slides.notes: E1: pancreas. E2: glucose units. E3: no calibrated clinical or individual information. Re-teach substance roles first if needed.

body: Sequence • substance roles • feedback • model limits.
slides.notes: Shared exit minute. Accept a labelled route and a spoken limit.

blocks.text: Role reminders: insulin is a hormone signal. Glucose is a sugar used by cells. Glycogen is a carbohydrate store made from joined glucose units. Some glucose uptake is insulin-independent; the model focuses on insulin-responsive tissues.

blocks.prompt: W1. Predict and order the core response. W2. Correct the substance swap. W3. State a model limit.

pupilPages.title: Supported route | Trace the corrective response
pupilPages.intro: Word bank: pancreas; insulin; blood; glucose; glycogen; uptake; towards.

blocks.prompt: S1. Order cards A–D and explain why B follows A.
S2. Identify the signal, the sugar and the store. Use insulin, glucose and glycogen once each.
S3. Explain how the target response can reduce raised blood glucose. Name one target tissue.
S4. Why does the extra insulin stimulus reduce as glucose returns towards usual levels? Give one limit of the model.

pupilPages.title: Standard route | Explain the control loop
pupilPages.intro: Use mechanisms rather than a story about a hormone choosing what to do.

blocks.prompt: M1. Explain the sequence from glucose absorption to pancreatic insulin release and target-tissue response.
M2. Distinguish insulin, glucose and glycogen, including why insulin does not become the stored material.
M3. Explain why this is a corrective feedback response, not an endlessly increasing output.
M4. Evaluate a claim that the model predicts an exact blood-glucose concentration over time. Identify two missing kinds of information.

pupilPages.title: Stretch route | Test the limits and optional second branch
pupilPages.intro: Optional deeper evaluation. T3 is Higher-tier only: lower blood glucose can stimulate pancreatic alpha cells to release glucagon; the liver releases glucose, including by glycogen breakdown.

blocks.prompt: T1. Explain why “all cells need insulin for all glucose uptake” is too broad. Give a better core statement.
T2. The same qualitative rise is shown for two fictional people. Must their timing or exact concentrations match? Explain.
T3. Optional Higher: sequence lower glucose → glucagon release → liver response → towards usual. Contrast it with the insulin branch.
T4. Suggest one feature this model would need to compare real measurements. Explain why adding that feature alone would not validate its predictions.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection | A signal is not a sugar
pupilPages.intro: Use precise words or labelled arrows.

blocks.prompt: E1. Which organ releases insulin into blood?
E2. Which material supplies the units stored as glycogen?
E3. What limits this model to a qualitative explanation rather than an exact concentration prediction?
L1. What did your audience question? Improve a label or causal explanation.

answers.label: Retrieval and We do
answers.answer: R1: blood; R2: respiration and material use/storage; R3: the original departure. W1: A→B→C→D. W2: glucose units, not insulin, are stored as glycogen; insulin signals the processes. W3: no exact concentrations, times or individual parameters are supplied.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: Correct: raised glucose stimulates more insulin release and uptake/storage responses. Insulin is not converted into glucose. The model supplies no dosing information.

answers.label: S1 / M1
answers.answer: After absorption raises blood glucose, pancreatic beta cells release more insulin into blood. Insulin-responsive tissues alter glucose handling; some body cells increase uptake and liver/muscle glycogen storage is promoted.

answers.label: S2 / M2
answers.answer: Insulin=chemical messenger hormone; glucose=sugar/material; glycogen=store of joined glucose units. A hormone signal changes cell processes; it is not the bulk material being stored.

answers.label: S3
answers.answer: Uptake by insulin-responsive tissues such as muscle and storage as glycogen in liver/muscle help remove glucose from blood, tending to reduce the raised concentration.

answers.label: S4 / M3
answers.answer: As glucose moves towards the suitable range, the stimulus for extra insulin release reduces. The response counteracts the original rise rather than amplifying it indefinitely.

answers.label: M4 / T2
answers.answer: No. The model has no calibrated concentrations, real time scale, individual physiology, absorption details or measured response parameters. Similar qualitative patterns need not have identical numerical values or timing.

answers.label: T1
answers.answer: Some tissues take up glucose through insulin-independent routes. Better: insulin promotes uptake/storage responses in particular tissues, including increased uptake in muscle cells; it does not control every uptake route in every cell.

answers.label: T3 optional Higher
answers.answer: Lower glucose stimulates pancreatic alpha cells to release glucagon. Glucagon promotes liver glucose release, including glycogen breakdown, tending to raise blood glucose towards usual levels. Insulin responds to raised glucose and promotes uptake/storage; both reduce their original departure. Core success does not require glucagon.

answers.label: T4
answers.answer: A time/concentration axis with defined units could support comparing measurements. The relationships and parameters would still need testing against independent measured data; adding an axis alone does not show the model predicts accurately for different individuals.

answers.label: Exit and assessment
answers.answer: E1: pancreas. E2: glucose units. E3: no calibrated concentration scale, real time scale or individual response parameters. L1: specific mechanism correction or justified confirmation. Secure core: correct insulin sequence, substance distinction and model limit.

teacherNotes: 40-minute lesson. Zero-minute slides share the preceding stage allocation.
Choose one response route. Accept accurate speech, pointing with explanation, annotations or writing; record the support used.
A teacher or TA can be a quiet audience: ask one evidence question, then let the pupil revise or justify a decision.
Core control panel remains qualitative and contains no blood-glucose values or doses. Advance only on a pupil or teacher action.
The Higher glucagon extension is separate and closed by default. It is never required to answer core insulin questions.
The paper route orders and explains the same A–D events. The animation represents an authored causal sequence, not a numerical physiology simulation.
